Question: As a Christian, did you know that the name Daniel is Islamic?
Answer: That would be odd indeed. The Book of Daniel was authored in the 2nd Century BC, probably around 165 BC, during the Maccabean revolt against the Seleucid Empire. The events in the Book of Daniel are supposed to have taken place in the 6th Century BC and Daniel is a Jew exiled in Babylon in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar. The book was originally written in Hebrew and Aramaic and appears in the Hebrew Bible, the Tanakh, specifically in the Ketuvim or Hagiographical section, between Esther and Ezra or between Lamentations and Esther. However, the Book of Ezekial, which may have been written as early as 570 BC, more contemporaneously with the supposed events, also mentions a DN’L (Hebrew words are written without vowels) which might, or might not, be a reference to the same Daniel. The Islamic period, on the other hand, dates from the 610, at least some 800 years later than the probable writing of the Book of Daniel. However, Daniel is recognised in the Shia branch of Islam as an imported prophet, although he is not mentioned in the Koran. Therefore, Daniel appears in the Jewish, Christian, and Islamic religious traditions, as well as making an appearance in The Thousand and One Nights as a twelve year old boy on Night 394, The pious Jewish woman and the two evil old men.

Question: Did Germany consider invading England after France surrendered and before The Battle of Britain?
Answer: No. The suppression of the RAF, aka the Battle of Britain, was considered a vital pre-condition for the launch of Unternehmen Seelöwe (Operation Sealion) the invasion of the British Isles. German shipping under attack by the RAF Führer Directive 16, issued in July 1940, set out four pre-conditions for the launching of Sealion. These four conditions were: All four were huge tasks and it was utterly beyond the capability of the Germans to achieve any of them in either the short or medium term. In any case the French signed the Armistice on the 25th June 1940 and the Battle of Britain started on the 10th of July 1940. The two weeks between the two events wasn’t anywhere remotely near sufficient time to plan, assemble, and launch an invasion. In any case, Führer Directive 16 wasn’t even issued until a week after the Battle of Britain started. A Squadron of Hurricanes Not only was an early invasion logistically completely impossible, any attempt to launch it would have been utterly slaughtered unless the RAF had been suppressed first.

Question: How did former colonies, such as Canada, react to Britain giving up control over them after World War II?
Answer: It’s so much more complicated than that. Britain didn’t give up control over Canada after WW2, it was a more nuanced process than that and extended over a long period of time. In reality Canada had a large measure of independence after 1867. During each of these steps, the provinces of Canada had various forms of legislature, operating with various degrees of success and various levels of authority. Effectively, Canada became largely self-governing with the British North America Act in 1867. The Act set up the House of Commons and Senate of Canada and delineated the powers of the Federal and Provincial governments. Canada remains part of the Commonwealth and recognises Charles III as King of Canada. As to the other colonies and dominions, there is no simple, universal, answer. Some sixty-five countries (according to Wikipedia) have gained independence from the United Kingdom over the last 250 years. Some have done very well and transitioned into full democracies whilst others have done less well. Name: Richard Meakin
Question: What do you think of Rheinmetall's goal to produce up to 1.1 million artillery shells a year by 2027?
Answer: It’s a start, but possibly too little too late, as several estimates suggest that the Russians are already producing around 3 million shells per year and still ramping up. The absolute number is irrelevant, it’s the ratio that matters. It’s going to be difficult for the NATO nations to compete whilst maintaining a peacetime economy if the Russians have moved to a wartime economy. NATO could certainly out produce Russia if it wanted to, it has a much larger economy even in PPP terms, but at what cost? What tax rises and cuts to services would be required to match or out-perform Russia? I notice that the MOD recently (Jan 2024) issued the following statement: The Ministry of Defence (MOD) placed an order in June 2023 with BAE Systems to provide an eight-fold increase in production capability of 155mm shells. Call me cynical, but those look like weasel words to me - shorthand for we’re increasing from virtually nothing to not very much - otherwise why not just state the number? I hope I’m wrong. I understand that a 155mm shell can cost anything between $1,000 and $100,000 depending on production volumes and on how smart it is (Excalibur for instance). Even with volume production and dumb shells, we’re talking about billions of dollars per year to outperform Russia and that’s before we start looking at the, much more expensive, missiles that we will also need to be producing in volume. In 1917, Britain produced over 76 million artillery shells. If things continue this way, it’s going to get expensive fast folks.

Question: I realize some of the Allied forces that invaded North Africa in WWII came from Europe, but wasn’t the bulk of the force launched from the US East Coast? How did the Allies handle logistics?
Answer: The invasion of French North Africa, Operation Torch, consisted of three task forces. Whilst, the Western Task Force (35,000 men) came directly from the United States, the Central Task Force (39,000 men) and Eastern Task Force (33,000 men) both departed from the United Kingdom. Therefore, a little under a third of the men involved in Torch, those of the Western Task Force targeting Casablanca in Morocco, came directly from the United States. Ships of the Western Task Force heading for Morocco The Western Task Force sailed mainly from Norfolk, Virginia, on the 24th of October 1942, in a convoy (Task Force 34/UGF 1) of 102 troop transports, cargo ships, tankers, and escorts, including the US carrier Ranger, three battleships (Texas, New York, and Massachusetts), four escort carriers, seven cruisers and thirty-eight destroyers, in addition to troop and cargo transports and auxiliaries, under Rear Admiral Henry Kent Hewitt on the cruiser Augusta. USS Barnett (APA-5) an Attack Transport, note the landing craft carried on her sides The logistics for the invasion itself were self-contained with cargo ships and tankers included in the invasion force. Following the initial invasion the troops were supplied by the UGF (United States to Gibraltar Fast) and UGS (United States to Gibraltar Slow) starting with UGF 2 on the 6th of November 1942 and ending on the 28th of May 1945. There were twenty-six UGF convoys totalling 382 ships and one hundred slow convoys totalling 5,800 ships. Some twenty-five of these ships were lost to U-boats, aircraft or mines.
